mainTopic: Whether a master must feed his slave (רב versus רבי יוחנן), and whether freedom is a benefit or a loss for a כהן's slave
overview: The גמרא finishes discussing רב's ruling about a master who is מקדיש his slave's hands. The slave borrows only for extra food, which the הקדש is happy to allow because it makes him stronger. He repays the loan with bits of work worth less than a פרוטה, which never become holy. From רב's two rulings, the גמרא concludes that according to רב a master cannot say to his slave, "Work for me, but I will not feed you." Then it brings רבי יוחנן's ruling about someone who cuts off a slave's hand: the master gets the payments and the slave lives on charity. From the exact word ניזון, the גמרא proves that רבי יוחנן holds a master can refuse to feed his slave. It also explains that even leftover medical money, saved because a harsh medicine healed the slave faster, goes to the master. Finally, a ברייתא records the debate between רבי מאיר and the Rabbis over whether freedom helps a כהן's slave or hurts him. The issue is that a freed slave loses the right to eat תרומה, while for a woman a גט is clearly a loss.

steps.title: Why would the slave need to borrow?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions how a slave who is fed by his master could need to borrow food.
steps.simpleTranslation: He borrows and eats? (His master already feeds him!)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's statement that the slave 'borrows and eats.' If his master supports him, why would he need to borrow?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The discussion is about a slave whose master provides his food. If he already has food, a loan seems pointless. So the גמרא wants to know what the loan is for.

keyTerms.meaning: something given to the בית המקדש; also the Temple treasury

phrases.english: He borrows and eats?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up רב's ruling from earlier on the daf and questions one detail of it.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's phrase 'borrows and eats,' in a case where the master feeds the slave
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone who is already fed has no need to borrow food.

steps.title: He borrows for extra food
steps.stepSummary: The slave borrows to pay for extra food beyond his basic needs.
steps.simpleTranslation: For surplus food, meaning extra food beyond what his master gives him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the loan pays for extra food, called העדפה, beyond the basics the master gives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The master covers the slave's basic needs, but the slave wants more. That extra food is what he borrows for.

keyTerms.meaning: surplus or extra, here meaning extra food beyond the basics

phrases.english: For surplus [food].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case to borrowing for extra food
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Borrowing makes no sense for a slave who is fed.
steps.terutzMaskana: He borrows only for extra food beyond his basic support.

steps.title: Why not tell him to manage without the extra?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the הקדש does not simply tell the slave that he can live without extra food, just as he always has.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the הקדש tell him: Until now you managed without extra food, so now too you can manage without extra food!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 2. The הקדש should be able to refuse the slave's request for extra food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slave never had extra food before, so the extra is not something he truly needs. If so, why should the הקדש have to let him work for it? It could keep all his work for itself.

keyTerms.meaning: and let him say to him

phrases.english: But let the Temple treasury say to him:
Until now it was enough for you
without surplus,
and now too let it be enough for you
without surplus!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the slave may work for extra food
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He has always lived without the extra, so the הקדש should be able to refuse it.

steps.title: The הקדש wants a stronger slave
steps.stepSummary: The הקדש itself is happy for the slave to eat more, because a better-fed slave is worth more.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הקדש itself is pleased with this, so that its slave will be improved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the הקדש actually wants the slave to eat extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Extra food makes the slave stronger, and a stronger slave is worth more and works better for the הקדש. So allowing the extra food helps the הקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: it is pleasing to him, he prefers it

phrases.english: The Temple treasury itself prefers it,
so that its slave will be improved.
phrases.notes: Since his hands belong to the הקדש, a stronger slave means more valuable work for it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that the הקדש benefits from the extra food
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The הקדש loses out by letting him have extra food, so it should refuse.
steps.terutzMaskana: The הקדש gains a stronger slave, so it wants him to have the extra.

steps.title: How can he repay if his work becomes holy?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the slave can work to pay back the loan, since everything his hands produce becomes holy as soon as it is made.
steps.simpleTranslation: He works and repays? But each bit of work becomes holy right away!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the next part of רב's ruling, that the slave 'works and repays.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: His hands were made holy, so each piece of work he does becomes הקדש the moment he does it. Then nothing is left over for him to give the lender.

keyTerms.meaning: each first bit, as soon as it is made

phrases.english: He works and repays?
Each bit immediately becomes consecrated!

steps.triggerLanguage: עוֹשֶׂה וּפוֹרֵעַ, קַמָּא קַמָּא קָדֵישׁ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new detail of רב's ruling: the repayment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Everything his hands produce becomes הקדש right away, so he has nothing of his own to repay with.

steps.title: Work worth less than a פרוטה stays his
steps.stepSummary: The slave works in amounts worth less than a פרוטה each, which do not become holy, and he repays with those.
steps.simpleTranslation: He does it in tiny amounts, each worth less than a פרוטה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that work worth less than a פרוטה does not become holy, so the slave can use it to repay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holiness does not take effect on something worth less than a פרוטה. The slave can gather these tiny amounts and pay back the loan bit by bit.

keyTerms.meaning: less than the value of a פרוטה, the smallest amount that counts in halacha

steps.whatToRemember: The slave borrows only for extra food, which the הקדש is happy to allow, and he repays with tiny amounts of work, each under a פרוטה, which never become holy.

phrases.english: With amounts each less than the value of a peruta.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Uses the minimum-value rule for הקדש
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All of his work becomes holy, so he cannot repay.
steps.terutzMaskana: Work worth less than a פרוטה does not become holy, so he repays with those small amounts.

steps.title: Support from another ruling of רב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows it makes sense that the borrowing case is about a slave whose master feeds him, because רב rules elsewhere that an unsupported slave simply works and eats.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is also logical, as רב said: When someone is מקדיש his slave's hands, that slave works and eats, because if the slave does not work, who will work for him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ruling of רב to support the idea that the borrowing case involves a slave who is fed by his master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this other ruling, רב says the slave works and eats directly. That must be a case where nobody else feeds him, since otherwise who would support him? So the earlier 'borrows and eats' ruling must be about a slave whose master feeds him and who borrows only for extras.

keyTerms.meaning: one who makes his slave's hands (his work) holy

steps.whatToRemember: רב has two rulings. A slave with no support works and eats directly. A slave whose master feeds him borrows for extras and repays in amounts under a פרוטה.

phrases.english: So too it is logical;
as Rav said:
One who consecrates the hands of his slave —
that slave works and eats,
for if the slave does not [work],
who will work for him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the basic case set up in steps 1 and 2 and supports it with another ruling of רב.
steps.raayaObject: That רב's 'borrows and eats' ruling is about a slave whose master feeds him
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב's other ruling that a slave whose hands were made holy works and eats, since otherwise no one would support him

steps.title: The two rulings of רב fit together if the borrowing case is about a fed slave
steps.stepSummary: If the borrowing ruling is about a slave whose master feeds him and cannot stop, and the 'works and eats' ruling is about a slave who is not fed, then רב's two rulings fit together nicely.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, if you say that this ruling is about a master who feeds his slave and cannot stop, and that ruling is about a master who does not feed him, everything works out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing the proof from step 7. It shows that one way of reading רב's two rulings fits together with no problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the borrowing case, the master feeds the slave and is not allowed to stop, so the הקדש on the slave's hands takes effect, and the slave must borrow to get extra food. In the 'works and eats' case, the master does not feed him, so the הקדש does not take effect and the slave keeps his earnings. Both rulings make sense under this reading.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted / it works out fine (opens the reading that has no problem)
Provides food for (the master supports the slave)
He cannot (the master cannot refuse to feed the slave)

phrases.english: Granted, if you say
that this one is where he provides food, and he cannot [stop],
phrases.notes: "This one" is רב's borrowing case. "He cannot" means the master cannot say, "Work for me, but I won't feed you."

phrases.english: and this one is where he does not provide food, it is fine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how step 7's proof works by showing that one reading fits both of רב's rulings together.
steps.raayaObject: That רב holds a master who feeds his slave cannot refuse to feed him.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב's two rulings: the slave borrows and repays, and the slave works and eats.

steps.title: The other reading makes רב's reason fall apart
steps.stepSummary: If the borrowing case were also about an unfed slave whose master can refuse to feed him, then רב's reason, "if he doesn't work, who will work for him?", would make no sense. Someone else could support him.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if you say this case is also where the master does not feed him, and he is allowed to refuse, then why say, "If he doesn't work, who will work for him?" Let whoever wants to work for him do so!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the other possible reading and shows it causes a problem with רב's reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a master is allowed to refuse to feed his slave, then the slave's survival is not the master's problem. The slave can live from charity. So רב's worry, "who will support him?", could not stop the הקדש from taking effect. This means the reading falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: But if you say (opens the reading that has a problem)
Let whoever wants to, work for him (others can support him)

phrases.english: But if you say
this one is where he does not provide food, and he can [refuse],

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי לָא עַבְדָּא מַאן פָּלַח לֵיהּ?!
phrases.english: [then why say] "For if he doesn't work, who will work for him?!"
Let whoever wants to, work for him!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִי אָמְרַתְּ הָךְ בְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ מַעֲלֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the 'granted, but' pattern started in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that a master can refuse to feed his slave.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the master may refuse, then רב's reason ("who will support him?") cannot explain why the הקדש fails, because others or charity could support the slave.

steps.title: Conclusion: according to רב, a master cannot refuse to feed his slave
steps.stepSummary: Since only the first reading works, the גמרא concludes that a master cannot say to his slave, "Work for me, but I will not feed you."
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, must we not learn from this that he cannot? Yes, learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the proof and accepts the result: a master אינו יכול refuse to feed his slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second reading broke רב's reasoning, so the first reading must be correct. That reading depends on the idea that a master who feeds his slave may not stop, so this is the conclusion.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not so that... (leads into the conclusion)
Learn from it (yes, this is the conclusion)

steps.whatToRemember: From רב's two rulings, the גמרא concludes that a master cannot say to his slave, "Work for me, but I will not feed you."

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לָאו, שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל!
phrases.english: Rather, must we not learn from this that he cannot?!
Learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the contrast between steps 8 and 9.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to רב, a master אינו יכול לומר לעבד עשה עמי ואיני זנך.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's case of the cut-off hand suggests a master can refuse to feed his slave
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that someone who cuts off another person's slave's hand pays the master for lost work and medical costs, while the slave lives on charity. This suggests the master is allowed to refuse to feed the slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, as רבי יוחנן said: one who cuts off the hand of his friend's slave gives the payment for lost work and the medical costs to the master, and that slave is fed from charity. Learn from this that a master can say to his slave, "Work for me, but I will not feed you"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source, from רבי יוחנן, that seems to prove the opposite of what we just concluded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the master had to feed his slave, the payment for lost work should go toward feeding the injured slave. Instead, the master keeps the money and the slave lives on charity. This shows the master has no duty to feed him, so a master יכול refuse.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (introduces a source to prove a point)
Payment for his lost work time
"Work for me, but I will not feed you"

steps.confusionAlert: This step seems to clash with step 10. Step 10 was רב's view taken from his own rulings, while this proof comes from רבי יוחנן and points the other way.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the question of feeding a slave is not settled by one source. Different אמוראים may hold different views.

phrases.english: Come and hear, as Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
One who cuts off the hand of his friend's slave –
gives the payment for his lost work and his medical costs to his master,
and that slave is fed from charity.

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ, יָכוֹל הָרַב לוֹמַר לָעֶבֶד:
phrases.english: Learn from this: the master can say to the slave:
"Work for me, but I will not feed you"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new source that points the opposite way from the conclusion in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: That a master can say to his slave, "Work for me, but I will not feed you."
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's ruling about someone who cuts off a slave's hand: the master receives the payments and the slave lives on charity.

steps.title: The master in רבי יוחנן's case does feed the slave
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from רבי יוחנן by saying his case is about a master who does provide food.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the master provides food for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the proof from step 11. It says רבי יוחנן was talking about a master who does feed his slave, so nothing can be proven from his ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 argued that if the slave lives on charity, his master must be allowed to stop feeding him. This answer cuts that link. In רבי יוחנן's case, the master really is feeding the slave.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? This phrase introduces a narrower reading of a case.

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
Where [the master] provides food for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the proof brought in step 11 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן's slave lives on charity, so his master must have been allowed to stop feeding him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The master does feed the slave. The case teaches nothing about whether a master may refuse.

steps.title: Then why does he need charity?
steps.stepSummary: If the master feeds him, why would the slave need to be supported by charity?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why is he sustained from charity?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. If the master is already feeding the slave, why does רבי יוחנן say the slave lives on charity?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's words say the slave is 'ניזון מן הצדקה', supported by charity. A slave whose master already feeds him should not need charity, so the answer seems to clash with the wording.

phrases.english: If so,
why is he sustained from charity?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אַמַּאי נִיזּוֹן מִן הַצְּדָקָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יוחנן's master feeds the slave.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A fed slave would not need charity, yet רבי יוחנן says he is sustained from charity.

steps.title: Charity is only for extras
steps.stepSummary: The charity covers extra food beyond what the master provides.
steps.simpleTranslation: For extras.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers in one word. The master gives the basics, and the charity is only for extra food the slave wants.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This tries to save the reading from step 12. The master still feeds the slave. Charity just adds on top of that, so the two do not clash.

phrases.english: For surplus.
phrases.notes: Extra food beyond the basics the master already gives.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Charity must mean the slave has no food from his master.
steps.terutzMaskana: Charity covers only extras. The master provides the basics.

steps.title: The word 'ניזון' does not fit extras
steps.stepSummary: If charity were only for extras, רבי יוחנן should have said 'מתפרנס', not 'ניזון'.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, would he say 'sustained'? He should have said 'earns a living'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the 'extras' answer by looking at רבי יוחנן's exact word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ניזון' means getting the food you need to live, which is basic support. For extras, the fitting word would be 'מתפרנס', making a living or getting more comfortable support. Since רבי יוחנן said 'ניזון', the charity must be his basic food.

keyTerms.meaning: Earns a living; gets fuller support

phrases.english: If so, [would he say] 'sustained'?!
He should have said 'earns a living'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Knocks down the answer of step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The 'extras' answer, and with it the reading that the master feeds the slave.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'ניזון' means basic food, not extras. Extras would be called 'מתפרנס'.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן holds the master may refuse to feed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that, according to רבי יוחנן, a master can say 'work for me but I won't feed you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, must we not conclude from this that he can? Conclude from this.
steps.whatsHappening: With the answers knocked down, the גמרא accepts the proof from step 11. According to רבי יוחנן, a master may refuse to feed his slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the charity is the slave's basic food, his master was not feeding him. That shows a master is allowed to refuse. 'שמע מינה' confirms that the proof stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it; the proof stands
He can; here, the master is able to refuse

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, a master can tell his slave, 'Work for me, but I will not feed you.' This is learned from his ruling that an injured slave lives on charity.
steps.confusionAlert: This is the opposite of what the גמרא concluded from רב in step 10. Keep the two straight: the conclusion in step 10 came from רב's rulings, and this one comes from רבי יוחנן's ruling.

phrases.english: Rather, must we not conclude from this that he can!
phrases.notes: 'He can' means the master can say, 'Work for me but I won't feed you.'

phrases.english: Conclude from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion now that the defense in steps 12–14 has failed.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יוחנן holds that a master may refuse to feed his slave.

steps.title: Payment for lost work obviously goes to the master
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יוחנן's ruling again and notes that paying the master for lost work is obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: He gives payment for lost work and medical costs to his master. Lost work is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to quote רבי יוחנן's ruling in order to study its details. It points out that the payment for lost work going to the master is obvious, which sets up the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slave's work belongs to the master. So of course the master gets paid for the time the slave cannot work. That raises the question of why this needed to be said at all.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said; introduces a quote of an earlier statement to discuss it
His loss of work time (from שֶׁבֶת, sitting idle)

steps.confusionAlert: 'שבתו' here has nothing to do with שבת the day. It means the time he 'sits idle' and cannot work.

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: He is quoting רבי יוחנן's ruling from step 11.

phrases.english: He gives his loss of work and his medical costs to his master.
His loss of work is obvious!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר מָר: נוֹתֵן שִׁבְתּוֹ וּרְפוּאָתוֹ לְרַבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the feeding question and studies the details of רבי יוחנן's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי יוחנן needed to mention payment for lost work, since it obviously goes to the master.

steps.title: The new point is the medical costs
steps.stepSummary: The real חידוש is that the medical costs also go to the master.
steps.simpleTranslation: His medical costs needed to be stated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יוחנן's real point was about the medical costs, not the lost work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lost work was mentioned only as part of the full list. The new teaching is that the money for healing also goes to the master.

keyTerms.meaning: It was necessary for him to say

phrases.english: His medical costs were necessary for him [to state].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The new teaching is that the payment for medical costs goes to the master.

steps.title: Isn't the medical money for the slave's own healing?
steps.stepSummary: Why should the master get the medical money? The slave needs it to get healed.
steps.simpleTranslation: His medical money is his, since he needs to be healed with it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that the medical costs go to the master. The money is for the slave's own treatment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lost work belongs to the master, but healing seems to belong to the injured person. The money should go toward curing the slave, not into the master's pocket.

phrases.english: His medical costs are his,
since he needs to be healed with it!

steps.triggerLanguage: רְפוּאָתוֹ דִּידֵיהּ הִיא, דְּבָעֵי אִיתַּסּוֹיֵי בֵּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the medical payment goes to the master.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Medical money exists to heal the slave, so it should belong to him.

steps.title: Leftover money after a fast, painful cure
steps.stepSummary: The case is a slave healed faster than expected by a harsh medicine. The leftover money still goes to the master, even though the slave suffered the pain.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where they estimated five days, they made him a strong medicine, and he healed in three days. You might say the pain was his, so the money is his. It teaches us that it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רבי יוחנן was talking about leftover medical money. The slave healed quickly with a strong, painful medicine, and the leftover money goes to the master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Of course the slave is treated with the money. The question is what happens to money left over when the cure was quicker and cheaper. Even though the slave paid for that savings with extra pain, רבי יוחנן teaches that the leftover goes to the master.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case
You might have said... so it teaches us otherwise

steps.whatToRemember: In רבי יוחנן's case, the injurer pays both lost work and medical costs to the master. Even money saved because a harsh medicine healed the slave faster goes to the master, although the slave suffered the pain.

phrases.english: No, it is needed where they estimated him at five days,
phrases.notes: Doctors estimated the wound would take five days to heal, and the injurer paid for that.

phrases.english: and they made him a strong medicine
and he was healed in three days;
you might have said:
the pain was his, [so the leftover money is his],
it teaches us [that it goes to the master].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19 by placing רבי יוחנן's ruling in a specific case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the slave suffered the pain of the strong medicine, the money saved should be his.
steps.terutzMaskana: The leftover medical money goes to the master.

steps.title: The Rabbis challenge רבי מאיר: freedom is a benefit
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי אלעזר: the Rabbis challenged רבי מאיר, saying that going free is surely good for a slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי אלעזר said: We said to מאיר: Isn't it a benefit for a slave to leave his master's control and go free?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא where the Rabbis argue against רבי מאיר. They say that freeing a slave is obviously good for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי מאיר holds that a master who sends a freedom document through a messenger can still take it back, because freeing the slave does not simply count as a favor to him. The Rabbis push back: you can do a favor for someone without asking him (זכין לאדם שלא בפניו), and freedom is the biggest favor a slave can get.

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Elazar said,
We said to Meir:
But isn't it a benefit for the slave
that he leaves his master's hands to freedom!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַרְנוּ לוֹ לְמֵאִיר: וַהֲלֹא זְכוּת הוּא לָעֶבֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: a ברייתא expanding the משנה's dispute between רבי מאיר and the Rabbis.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's view that accepting a freedom document for a slave is not a benefit.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Freedom is obviously good for a slave, so anyone should be able to accept it for him.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: a כהן's slave loses תרומה
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר answers that freedom can hurt a slave: a כהן's slave who goes free can no longer eat תרומה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to us: It is a loss for him. If he was a כהן's slave, freeing him takes away his right to eat תרומה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר defends himself. He shows a case where freedom actually costs the slave something.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כהן's slave counts as part of the כהן's household, so he may eat תרומה. Once freed, he is a regular Jew and may not. So freedom is not a pure benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: A loss, something against his interest
A slave owned by a כהן
The portion of produce that only כהנים and their households may eat

phrases.english: He said to us: It is a loss for him –
for if he was a priest's slave,
it disqualifies him from eating teruma.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a real loss that comes with freedom
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Freedom is only good for a slave.
steps.terutzMaskana: For a כהן's slave, freedom costs him his right to eat תרומה, so it is a חוב.

steps.title: The Rabbis: the master doesn't have to feed him anyway
steps.stepSummary: The Rabbis reply that the master may refuse to feed the slave, so losing the master's food is no real loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: We said to him: But if the master wants, he is allowed not to feed him and not to support him!
steps.whatsHappening: The Rabbis push back on רבי מאיר's answer. The master doesn't have to give the slave food, so what is the slave really losing?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects to what we just learned from רבי יוחנן: a master may say 'work for me but I won't feed you.' The Rabbis argue that since the slave never had a guaranteed right to the master's תרומה, freeing him takes nothing away from him.

keyTerms.meaning: To support him (give him what he needs to live)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַרְנוּ לוֹ: וַהֲלֹא מָה אִם יִרְצֶה
phrases.english: We said to him: But what if he wants
not to feed him and not to support him? He is allowed!
phrases.notes: "He" is the master. This matches רבי יוחנן's rule from step 16.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַרְנוּ לוֹ: וַהֲלֹא מָה אִם יִרְצֶה שֶׁלֹּא לְזוּנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי מאיר's answer in step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's claim that losing תרומה makes freedom a חוב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The master can refuse to feed the slave at all, so the slave has no guaranteed food from the master to lose.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: a runaway slave still eats תרומה
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר answers that the right to eat תרומה doesn't depend on the master feeding him. A runaway slave or a rebellious wife still eats תרומה, but a freed slave does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to us: Think of a כהן's slave who ran away, or a כהן's wife who rebelled against her husband. Don't they still eat תרומה? But this freed slave does not eat it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר explains that the loss is not about food from the master. It is about the right to eat תרומה at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a slave who ran away, and so gets nothing from his master, may still eat תרומה from other כהנים. That right comes from his status, not from being fed. Freedom takes away the status itself, so the slave loses something real.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two kinds of loss. The Rabbis talked about food from the master. רבי מאיר is talking about the right to eat תרומה from anyone.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָנוּ: וּמָה אִילּוּ עֶבֶד כֹּהֵן שֶׁבָּרַח,
phrases.english: He said to us: And what about a priest's slave who ran away,
and a priest's wife who rebelled against her husband –
don't they eat teruma?
But this one does not eat it.
phrases.notes: "This one" is the slave who was freed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָנוּ: וּמָה אִילּוּ עֶבֶד כֹּהֵן שֶׁבָּרַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Separates two different rights: being fed versus having the status to eat תרומה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The slave's tie to תרומה depends on the master feeding him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The right to eat תרומה comes from status. Freedom removes that status, so it is a חוב.

steps.title: For a woman, a גט is clearly a loss
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by saying that for a woman a גט is definitely a חוב: she loses תרומה and also her support.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a woman: a גט is a loss for her, because it takes away her right to eat תרומה and makes her lose her support.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא states the woman's case. Unlike the slave, there is no question here: a גט hurts her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wife loses two things with a גט: תרומה (if married to a כהן) and the food her husband must give her. A master does not have to feed his slave, but a husband does have to feed his wife. So for her, the loss is double and certain. This is why everyone agrees a גט cannot be accepted for a woman without her.

keyTerms.meaning: Support and food a husband must give his wife

steps.whatToRemember: Slave: the Rabbis say freedom is a זכות, and רבי מאיר says it can be a חוב because of תרומה. Woman: a גט is clearly a חוב (she loses תרומה and מזונות).

phrases.english: But a woman – it is a loss for her,
since it disqualifies her from teruma
and makes her lose her support.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the ברייתא by contrasting the woman with the slave.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a woman, a גט is a חוב because she loses both תרומה and מזונות.

steps.title: How are the two sides answering each other?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the Rabbis were saying and how רבי מאיר's reply fits, since one side talks about food and the other about תרומה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What were they saying to him, and what was he answering them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to look closely at the ברייתא. It seems the two sides are talking about different things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Rabbis spoke about food (the master doesn't have to feed him). רבי מאיר answered with תרומה (a runaway still eats it). The גמרא wants to understand how these fit together as a real back-and-forth.

keyTerms.meaning: What were they saying to him?

phrases.english: What are they saying to him,
and what is he answering them?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָאָמְרוּ לֵיהּ, וּמַאי קָא מַהְדַּר לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes the exchange in steps 23-24.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How רבי מאיר's answer about תרומה responds to the Rabbis' point about food.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: you answered food, not תרומה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבי מאיר was saying: you answered my point about food, but what about תרומה?
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he was telling them: You answered me about food. What will you answer me about תרומה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבי מאיר's reply. He agrees the master doesn't have to feed the slave, but says that doesn't solve the תרומה problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר admits the Rabbis' point about food is correct. His real concern was never food. It is the right to eat תרומה, which a freed slave loses no matter who feeds him.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he was saying to them

phrases.english: This is what he is saying to them:
You have answered me about food,
what will you answer me about teruma?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר לְהוּ: הֲשַׁבְתּוּנִי עַל הַמְּזוֹנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי מאיר agreed about food but held that the loss of תרומה still makes freedom a חוב.

steps.title: But the master can free him anyway
steps.stepSummary: Still explaining רבי מאיר, the גמרא has him raise a possible objection: the master could throw the freedom document to the slave himself, so the slave would lose תרומה anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will say: If the master wants, he can throw a גט to the slave and disqualify him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר, as the גמרא explains his words, sees a possible objection coming and raises it himself. He answers it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument: the master can free the slave whenever he wants by throwing the document near him. So the slave's right to תרומה was never safe, and a messenger accepting the גט doesn't really hurt him.

keyTerms.meaning: He throws him a document (here, a freedom document)

phrases.english: And if you will say:

phrases.aramaic: אִי בָּעֵי, זָרֵיק לֵיהּ גִּיטָּא וּפָסֵיל לֵיהּ;
phrases.english: if he wants, he throws him a document and disqualifies him;
phrases.notes: "He" is the master. Here גט means the slave's freedom document.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימְרוּ: אִי בָּעֵי, זָרֵיק לֵיהּ גִּיטָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבי מאיר's words from step 27: he raises the Rabbis' expected rebuttal to his תרומה argument so that he can answer it.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's claim that the slave loses something when a messenger accepts his freedom.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The master can free him directly anytime, so the slave's תרומה was never secure.

steps.title: The slave can run away first
steps.stepSummary: The slave can stop the master from freeing him by running away, and so keep eating תרומה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He can leave him, run away, and go off into the world.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר answers the rebuttal he raised in step 28. The slave can protect himself from being freed by running away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To free the slave by throwing the document, the master must get it to him. If the slave runs off, the master can't reach him, and as we saw, a runaway still eats תרומה. But when a messenger accepts the גט, the slave has no chance to escape. So the messenger really is causing a loss.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי מאיר, a messenger accepting a freedom document for a כהן's slave causes a real loss. The master could free him himself, but the slave could avoid that by running away and keep eating תרומה.

phrases.english: he can leave him, and run away, and go off into the world.
phrases.notes: The slave runs away before the master can throw him the document. A runaway still eats תרומה, as we saw in step 24.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the slave could have avoided the loss, so the messenger really causes it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the master can free him anyway, the slave loses nothing when a messenger accepts it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The slave could run away and keep his תרומה rights. The messenger's acceptance takes that option away, so it is a חוב.
